candidates.text: The Framers gave Congress the power to regulate commerce, not to compel it, and for over 200 years both our decisions and Congress's actions have reflected this understanding
candidates.speaker: Roberts
phrases: the power to regulate commerce, not to compel it
candidates.reason: States the activity/inactivity limit on the commerce power that the Critique's scholarship (Barnett; Harvard Law Review Note) treats as the case's central doctrinal move.

candidates.text: In this case, the financial `inducement' Congress has chosen is much more than `relatively mild encouragement'---it is a gun to the head
candidates.speaker: Roberts (plurality)
phrases: economic dragooning that leaves the States with no real option
it is a gun to the head
candidates.reason: States the Spending Clause coercion rule, the decision's most consequential new limit (Greve; coverage-gap critiques).

candidates.text: The Affordable Care Act's requirement that certain individuals pay a financial penalty for not obtaining health insurance may reasonably be characterized as a tax
candidates.speaker: Roberts
phrases: may reasonably be characterized as a tax
candidates.reason: The taxing-power holding that sustained the mandate.

candidates.text: The Chief Justice's crabbed reading of the Commerce Clause harks back to the era in which the Court routinely thwarted Congress' efforts
candidates.speaker: Ginsburg
phrases: crabbed reading of the Commerce Clause

candidates.text: The Act before us here exceeds federal power both in mandating the purchase of health insurance and in denying non-consenting States all Medicaid funding
candidates.speaker: Joint dissent
phrases: it must follow that the entire statute is inoperative
